subject: business-studies
title: BCG Matrix and Brand Management
welcome_lead: Balance your portfolio with the BCG matrix and protect your brand equity.
meta_desc: A-Level Marketing: BCG matrix quadrants and brand management.
final_note: A balanced portfolio funds tomorrow's stars from today's cash cows.

concepts.def: High market share in a high-growth market.
High share in a low-growth market - generates cash.
Low share in a high-growth market - needs investment.
Low share in a low-growth market - candidate for divestment.
Added value a brand name brings beyond the functional product.
Using an existing brand to launch into a new product category.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Boston matrix plots relative market share against market growth. Stars are tomorrow's cash cows; question marks need funding; cash cows fund the future; dogs may be sold.
A strong brand creates customer loyalty, supports premium pricing and reduces marketing costs over time. Brand equity is built through consistent quality, communication and experience.
Brand extension leverages trust but can dilute the parent brand - think Colgate's frozen meals failure. Extensions work best where the brand promise transfers to the new category.

mcqs.q: A product with low market share in a low-growth market is a:
options: Star
Cash Cow
Question Mark
Dog

mcqs.q: Cash cows are typically used to:
options: Be sold off immediately
Fund question marks and stars
Compete on price with dogs
Replace existing customers

mcqs.q: What is a brand in marketing?
options: Taylor invented the assembly line at Ford.
A brand is the company that makes a product.
A brand is just the logo on a product.
A combination of name, design, symbols and associations that distinguishes a product and creates customer perception and loyalty — more than just a logo.

mcqs.q: What four growth strategies does Ansoff's Matrix identify?
options: A brand is the company that makes a product.
Ansoff's Matrix is about analysing competitors.

Market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), product development (new product, existing market), diversification (new product, new market).
Ansoff's Matrix shows market share against profit.
